name: runit
desc: Collection of tools for managing UNIX services
why: A minimal init and service supervisor from the daemontools lineage, a small door into how Unix systems boot and keep processes alive.

brief.what_it_is: runit is a cross-platform UNIX init scheme with service supervision, meant as a replacement for sysvinit and other init schemes. Its programs are runit (run as process 1), runit-init (installed as /sbin/init replacement), runsvdir, runsvchdir, runsv, sv, svlogd, chpst and utmpset. Input is a service directory of run scripts; output is supervised long-running processes, with logging through svlogd and runlevel changes via runsvchdir. It runs on GNU/Linux, *BSD, MacOSX, Solaris, and can be adapted to other Unix systems.
brief.why_it_exists: The author presents it as a reliable, small replacement for sysvinit that handles booting, running and shutting down in three stages, and that keeps the code in process no 1 minimal. The homepage says runit is optimized for reliability and small size.
brief.how_it_works: At boot, runit-init starts runit, which runs /etc/runit/1 (one-time initialization, with full control of /dev/console for an emergency shell), then /etc/runit/2 (normally runsvdir, which should not return until halt or reboot and is restarted if it crashes), then /etc/runit/3 on halt or reboot. runsvdir starts one runsv supervisor per service directory entry, and runsv keeps each service's run script alive, with a log/ subdirectory piped through svlogd. Runlevels are handled through runsvdir and runsvchdir, and service dependencies are resolved automatically per the homepage.

brief.install_notes: Default install is into /package (root needed to create it); the install page describes a manual non-root alternative where you copy command/runit* to /sbin and other command/ programs to /bin, or to $HOME/bin as non-root. Releases are tarballs (the install page names runit-2.3.1.tar.gz with a sha256sum), and you report success by mail to a listed address. Replacing init is a separate step covered by a 'How to replace init' page. Per the Homebrew metadata (not the homepage), the service directory is $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/var/service instead of /service, and runsvdir can be started manually with -P pointing there.
brief.standout: It is a init-plus-supervisor in one small toolkit from the daemontools lineage, with a three-stage boot model that is easy to read in shell scripts. The homepage itself is a plain, old-school document with real 2002 process listings from a Debian server, which is a window into how Unix systems have kept processes alive.
brief.status: Quiet. The homepage and install page reference release 2.3.1 but show no release date or last-commit date, and the homepage points to a GitHub repo for contributions. The author is G. Pape. Unknown exact date of last activity from the pages I read.
brief.caveats: Not a drop-in init on macOS: the Homebrew formula says it does not install runit as a replacement for init, and that some managed services may need to start as root. The install page assumes a /package directory and needs manual tweaks on MacOSX and some *BSD systems. The example outputs on the homepage are from 2002 Debian sarge systems. Discussion is on a mailing list, and the author asks people not to contact him privately. Licence not seen in the pages I read.

The program runit is intended to run as Unix process no 1, it is automatically started by the runit-init /sbin/init-replacement if this is started by the kernel.

entry.title: runit
entry.tldr: A tiny init and service supervisor from the daemontools lineage, showing how Unix boots and keeps daemons alive with a few shell scripts.
entry.deeper_look:
runit is an init scheme with service supervision, built as a small replacement for sysvinit and similar systems. It is a handful of programs: runit runs as process 1, runsvdir starts one runsv supervisor per entry in a service directory, and runsv keeps that service's run script alive. If the service dies, it is started again.

Boot is three stages, each a plain script. Stage 1 (/etc/runit/1) does one-time setup, with control of the console for an emergency shell. Stage 2 (/etc/runit/2) normally runs runsvdir, which should not return until halt or reboot, and is restarted if it crashes. Stage 3 (/etc/runit/3) runs on halt or reboot. The homepage states the goal: "runit is optimized for reliability and small size. The amount of code in process no 1 should be minimal."

The idea underneath is that a service is just a directory with a run script, and a supervisor is a small loop that restarts it. Logging goes through a log/ subdirectory piped to svlogd. Runlevels are handled with runsvdir and runsvchdir. Once that clicks, much of how Unix systems keep processes alive stops being mysterious.

The homepage is an old-school document that includes real process listings from 2002 Debian sarge servers. That is old, and fine for reading, because the model has barely changed.
entry.install:
brew install runit
# Homebrew does not install runit as an init replacement. The service directory is $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/var/service. Start a supervisor by hand with: runsvdir -P $HOMEBREW_PREFIX/var/service (may need root, depending on the services).
